description_full: The Walt Disney Company operates as an entertainment company in Americas, Europe, and the Asia Pacific. It operates in three segments: Entertainment, Sports, and Experiences. The company produces and distributes film and television content under the ABC Television Network, Disney, Freeform, FX, Fox, National Geographic, and Star brand television channels, as well as ABC television stations and A+E television networks; and produces original content under the Disney Branded Television, FX Productions, Lucasfilm, Marvel, National Geographic Studios, Pixar, Searchlight Pictures, Twentieth Century Studios, 20th Television, and Walt Disney Pictures banners. It also provides direct-to-consumer streaming services through Disney+, Disney+ Hotstar, and Hulu; sports-related video streaming content through ESPN, ESPN on ABC, ESPN+ DTC, and Star; sale/licensing of film and episodic content to television and video-on-demand services; theatrical, home entertainment, and music distribution services; DVD and Blu-ray discs, electronic home video licenses, and VOD rental services; staging and licensing of live entertainment events; and post-production services. In addition, the company operates theme parks and resorts, such as Walt Disney World Resort, Disneyland Resort, Disneyland Paris, Hong Kong Disneyland Resort, Shanghai Disney Resort, Disney Cruise Line, Disney Vacation Club, National Geographic Expeditions, and Adventures by Disney, as well as Aulani, a Disney resort and spa in Hawaii. Further, it licenses its intellectual property (IP) to a third party that owns and operates Tokyo Disney Resort; licenses trade names, characters, visual, literary, and other IP for use on merchandise, published materials, and games; operates a direct-to-home satellite distribution platform; sells branded merchandise through retail, online, and wholesale businesses; and develops and publishes books, comic books, and magazines. The company was founded in 1923 and is based in Burbank, California.

financial_summary: Walt Disney Company (The) is a mega-cap communication services business with a $201.5B market cap on $102.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $10.6B in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.95× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.5× net debt/EBITDA.

Management returns a meaningful 5.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.

val: The stock trades only 5% below its DCF fair value of $124, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 24%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $66.21 to $223 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Communication Services peers: P/E 21.0 vs 14.1 and P/FCF 19.1 vs 10.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 13% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.8% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 9% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.6%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.27).

Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.95x.

hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.5x net debt to EBITDA ($6.7B of cash against $44.5B of debt).
The current ratio of 0.74 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 36% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.8% over 3 years and 8.7% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 27% of profits supports about 2.3% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 39.7% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.02, a backlog worth 18% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 15%.
Capex runs 1.6x depreciation (8.5% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 79%.

It returns 5.8% a year to shareholders (4.5% in buybacks and 1.7% in dividends).

people: With about 180,180 employees, each generates about $568K of revenue, in line with the Communication Services median, and revenue has grown 5.7% a year across its filed history.
